verdicts.title: Coin flips are positional and invariant to the canary pool, enabling silent audit invalidation under key reuse
verdicts.reasoning: Every mechanical fact reproduces (I ran it): _coin_flip.py:353-358 derives the positional mask from fold_in(key, 'opaque.auditing.coin_flip') only, so mask(full)==mask(poolA)==mask(poolB) is True, the mask is prefix-stable across num_canaries (mask[:100] of m=200 == mask of m=100), and adding one pool element flipped 45 of the 99 shared records' in/out labels. But none of that establishes a library defect. (a) The inflation demo is self-cheating, not a defect: the record->coin map is NOT pool-invariant - coins are bound to records only through rng.choice over the pool, so the map is only computable AFTER the pool is fixed, and the demo's 'zero-leakage mechanism' is scores set equal to the coins. Any auditor who deliberately correlates canary content with coins they already hold the key for breaks one-run validity in every implementation, including the reference one; Steinke et al. Thm 5.2 assumes an honest auditor draws the coins independently of the canaries, and the library supports exactly that ordering (coin_flip is called on a dataset that already exists). docs/user-guide/auditing.md:273-277 states the obligation explicitly ('Fix the pool before target training, independently of that run's membership coins and outputs; do not construct CoinFlip directly to choose a favourable in/out mask'). (b) The drift scenario is ordinary seeded-reproducibility semantics under a user error the same docs paragraph forbids ('Use the same audited dataset for coin_flip, subset construction, and scoring'): changing candidate_indices changes both the selection and the labels, exactly as any seeded partition does. The coin stream is correctly domain-separated from mechanism keys (test_audit.py:440-467 asserts three distinct roots; test_stream_root_namespacing.py enumerates both auditing tags). There is a legitimate design improvement available - deriving each coin as fold_in(coin_root, record_index) so pool drift only perturbs the added/removed records instead of half the pool - but that is hardening, not a defect, and no honest documented usage produces a wrong epsilon.
verdicts.corrected_failure_scenario: No honest-usage failure established. Reproduced facts: the positional in/out mask is a pure function of (key, num_canaries) and is byte-identical across candidate_indices values and prefix-stable across num_canaries; because coins are attached to records positionally through the pool-dependent selection permutation, editing the pool by one element reassigns in/out for ~half the shared records (45/99 measured). Both consequences require the caller to violate an explicitly documented obligation - correlating canary content with coins they hold the key for, or recreating the partition against a drifted pool - and neither is reachable from the documented workflow. The available hardening is identity-bound coin derivation (fold_in(coin_root, record_index)), which would localize drift; the current design is not itself incorrect.

verdicts.title: loss_scores/gradient_scores silently score a wrong dataset when canary indices happen to be in range
verdicts.reasoning: Reproduced verbatim on this tree. With a 20-record dataset, cf = coin_flip(ds, num_canaries=4, key=key(3), candidate_indices=range(0,4)) gives canary_indices [0 1 2 3], out=[2]; scoring against cf.train_subset(ds) (len 19) returned [-0., -1., -9., -16.] instead of the correct [-0., -1., -4., -9.], and one_run accepted it: OneRunEstimate(n_in=3, n_out=1, auc=0.6667) with no error. The chain holds: _helpers.py:79-81 indexes whatever object it is handed, _scoring_loader (:137-156) validates only batch_size and reference_scores types, and CoinFlip (_coin_flip.py:136-157) stores no dataset size or fingerprint, so a one-line len(dataset) == dataset_size guard is unavailable. Severity stays low and I moved affects_epsilon to false: this is a caller mistake against an explicitly documented contract - loss_scores' docstring says 'dataset: The full dataset the partition was created from' and docs/user-guide/auditing.md:276-277 says 'Use the same audited dataset for coin_flip, subset construction, and scoring' - and it changes only an empirical audit estimate under that mistake, never a mechanism's guarantee. The finding's real content is the missing cheap defensive check, and the observation that head-placed pools (the crafted-canary layout PR #751 enables) turn a loud IndexError into silent corruption is accurate.
verdicts.corrected_failure_scenario: A caller passes the wrong dataset object to loss_scores/gradient_scores - most plausibly cf.train_subset(audited) instead of audited, which the crafted-canary workflow makes easy by putting two dataset objects in flight. _IndexedCanaries indexes the supplied object with the partition's canary indices, so when the pool sits near the head of the dataset the removed out-canaries shift Subset positions and every canary is scored against a different record. Reproduced: wrong scores [-0.,-1.,-9.,-16.] vs correct [-0.,-1.,-4.,-9.], accepted by one_run as OneRunEstimate(n_in=3, n_out=1, auc=0.6667) with no warning. With a tail pool the same mistake raises IndexError, so the hazard is invisible while following the documented layout. Impact is a wrong empirical audit number under a documented-contract violation, not a change to any mechanism's privacy guarantee; the fix is to record dataset size (or a fingerprint) on CoinFlip and check it in _scoring_loader.

verdicts.title: Lambda-CGD noise stream is unrooted: fold_in(key, step) collides with the caller's documented key space (missed by fix #728)
verdicts.reasoning: Reproduced end to end through the public API on this tree. _lambda_cgd.py:280 does current_key = rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, step) and :292 prev_key = rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, step - 1) with no string root, while every sibling mechanism roots itself (_engine.py:396 rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, MF_GAUSSIAN_STREAM_FOLD, 'mf_gaussian_column', step); _gaussian.py:407; _adaptive.py:113; _second_moment.py:92,101). The public path is unguarded: mf_gaussian_noise validates the key type and passes it verbatim (_mf_gaussian_noise.py:131-139) to _make_raw_mf_noise (:231-237), which hands it straight to LambdaCgdStrategy.raw_noise_factory (:152-169). BiSR is the only other raw_noise_factory and it routes through _matrix_factorization_noise (_bisr.py:131-137), which is rooted - so lambda-CGD is the sole surviving instance. split(key, n) is exactly (fold_in(key, i)) (random/_engine.py:118-127), so the mechanism's step keys ARE keys the caller gets from an ordinary derivation. Live repro: mf_gaussian_noise(zeros template, lambda_cgd_strategy(lambda_=0.5, normalized=False), n_steps=4, noise_multiplier=1.0, key=key(42)) step-0 noise is tensor([0.9301, 0.2699, 0.5048, -1.2086, -0.0477]) and torch.randn(5, generator=generator_from_key(split(key(42),2)[0])) is byte-identical (torch.equal True). The guard test cannot see it: test_stream_root_namespacing.py:26-63 enumerates only declared string constants and lambda-CGD declares none. docs/reference/rng.md:214-222 additionally asserts the tag 'opaque.dpftrl.mf_gaussian' is occupied by mf_gaussian_noise, which is false for this strategy - a careful reader is told the stream is rooted when it is not. Two corrections to the report: no in-repo default collides (the trainer's DP-FTRL branch passes key(a.seed) at _dp_trainer.py:1576 and adaptive-clipping quantile noise is string-rooted, and MF rejects adaptive clipping anyway), so exploitation needs caller-side key reuse; and 'restarting with the same key replays the noise' is true of every deterministically seeded mechanism, not specific to lambda-CGD, so I dropped it. Kept at high: an unrooted privacy-noise stream on a public path violates a documented, test-guarded invariant the repo already shipped a breaking fix (#728) to establish, and nothing - test, error, or accountant - reports the collision.
verdicts.corrected_failure_scenario: A caller uses lambda-CGD through the public factory - mf_gaussian_noise(params, lambda_cgd_strategy(...), n_steps=T, noise_multiplier=nm, key=base) - and, following docs/reference/rng.md:224-227, derives their own torch generators from the same base with integer folds (split(base) or fold_in(base, step)) for dropout, augmentation, a second mechanism, or any logged/released random quantity. Because _lambda_cgd.py:280 derives the DP noise generator as fold_in(base, step) with no mechanism root, those streams are byte-identical to the privacy noise: verified live, step-0 noise == torch.randn(5, generator=generator_from_key(split(key(42),2)[0])). If the colliding caller-side stream is observable, the injected DP noise for that step is exactly recoverable and the guarantee for the affected releases is void, with no warning, error, or accounting signal. No shipped Opaque path collides today (the trainer's other torch streams are string-rooted), so this is a latent public-API defect rather than a live epsilon loss; the fix is one line - root the stream with a namespaced tag, add it to the rng.md table and to test_stream_root_namespacing.py - and is breaking for reproducibility of existing lambda-CGD runs.

verdicts.title: Samplers seed numpy RNG from the raw key with no domain separation (same defect class as #728, sibling surface)
verdicts.reasoning: The code facts are exactly as stated and the surface is slightly larger than reported: np.random.default_rng is seeded from a bare key.seed at dpsgd/_poisson.py:108, dpftrl/_poisson.py:111, dpftrl/_b_min_sep.py:73, dpftrl/_balls_in_bins.py:103 and dpsgd/_k_out_of_t.py:58, and from an integer-only fold at dpsgd/_random_allocation.py:125. Under the convention fold_in's own docstring states (random/_engine.py:71-83, 'A mechanism that draws randomness folds one unique string tag into the key it was given') and docs/reference/rng.md:208-222 (whose tag table lists no sampler), samplers are mechanisms that draw randomness and are unrooted. The mitigations the reporter lists all check out: the trainer builds one sampler per run from key(a.data_seed or a.seed) with a string fold only on the ignore_data_skip restart path (_dp_trainer.py:3686-3703), and the torch-side noise streams go through generator_from_key (seed % MAX_TORCH_SEED into a torch Generator), a different PRNG family from numpy's PCG64, so no in-repo default draws a colliding stream. I moved affects_epsilon to false: unlike finding 68 there is no path where an honest caller's stream aliases a sampler's, the amplification analysis does not depend on the sampling stream being unpredictable to the key holder, and the reporter's own scenarios are either contrived (publishing default_rng(fold_in(key, epoch).seed) output) or benign (two samplers seeded identically is what a caller comparing samplers would want). Real content: a convention/hygiene deviation that the namespacing guard test structurally cannot see, worth fixing alongside 68 while the tag table is being edited.
verdicts.corrected_failure_scenario: All samplers seed numpy from the caller's key with no mechanism root, so two samplers constructed from one key draw the identical PCG64 stream (perfectly correlated participation patterns), and RandomAllocationSampler's per-epoch assignment stream is byte-identical to a caller's own np.random.default_rng(fold_in(key, epoch).seed). This is a documented-convention violation (rng.md:208-210 requires a unique string root per randomness-drawing mechanism; the tag table lists no sampler) that the stream-root guard test cannot detect. No in-repo path collides - the trainer builds one sampler per run and the torch noise streams use a different PRNG family - and no realistic honest usage turns this into a wrong or unsound epsilon, so the impact is reproducibility/hygiene, not privacy loss.

verdicts.title: _compile_with_fullgraph_fallback catches every Exception on first call, masking non-compile failures as compile fallbacks
verdicts.reasoning: The code is exactly as cited: _dp_trainer.py:203-223 compiles with fullgraph=True, and the wrapper's first-call handler is a bare 'except Exception as e' that logs 'torch.compile fullgraph=True failed (%s: %s); falling back to fullgraph=False for subsequent steps.' and then immediately re-executes the whole step under a fresh fullgraph=False compile. So any first-call exception - OOM, a data-dependent RuntimeError, a bug in the user's loss closure - is reported to the user as a torch.compile failure and the step body runs twice. The consequences the reporter claims are real but bounded: a genuine error re-raises from the fallback (so nothing is permanently swallowed except a first-call-only transient), and I confirmed the double execution is harmless to privacy state - the compiled callable is the vmap(grad)+clip transform produced by _create_grad_fn (:4121-4123, :4125-4145), whose clipping/noise state is threaded functionally and whose adaptive-clipping quantile keys are derived from the step counter rather than a live generator, so re-running the same call reproduces the same randomness. The OOM interaction is the only substantive harm: the trainer's collective OOM handling only sees the exception re-raised from the fallback, i.e. after a second full execution on an already-exhausted allocator. Note the docstring (:192-201) frames the broad catch as deliberate; narrowing it is awkward in practice because torch.compile surfaces failures as Unsupported, BackendCompilerFailed, InternalTorchDynamoError and plain RuntimeError. Confirmed as a diagnosability/robustness defect at low severity, not a correctness bug.
verdicts.corrected_failure_scenario: With torch_compile=True, any exception raised the first time the fullgraph=True grad transform executes is caught by the bare 'except Exception' at _dp_trainer.py:213, logged as a torch.compile fullgraph failure, and the entire step is re-run under a freshly compiled fullgraph=False variant. On a first-step OOM (the realistic case on MPS) the user is pointed at compile flags rather than memory, and the retry re-executes the full forward/backward on an already-exhausted allocator before the trainer's OOM handling ever sees the error; a first-call-only transient is absorbed entirely behind a misleading warning. No DP state is corrupted by the double execution - the compiled transform is functional and its RNG derivations are step-indexed, so the retry reproduces identical clipping and noise - so the impact is misdirected debugging plus doubled peak-memory pressure at exactly the wrong moment.

verdicts.title: StepPerf.memory_peak_gb on MPS is the run-wide reserved high-water, not the per-step peak its docstring claims
verdicts.reasoning: Verified by reading all three cited sites. _memory.py:162-178 sets peak_gb = torch.mps.driver_allocated_memory() (the driver's reserved high-water, which the in-file comment states does not shrink on free) and marks exact_peak=True; _memory.py:410-415 gates the per-step reset on device_capabilities(device).peak_memory_trackable, and _capabilities.py:124 returns device_type == 'cuda', so the reset never runs on MPS; the comment right above the gate is candid ('there peak_gb accumulates as the run's reserved high-water, and max_peak_memory_gb across steps gives the run peak'). The public StepPerf docstring at :275 nonetheless says 'memory_peak_gb: Peak GPU memory during the step', and that value flows into to_dict() (:305), the distributed max-reduce (_distributed.py:40-44), and the wandb example in the module docstring, so per-step MPS logs carry a monotone run-cumulative number under a per-step label while CUDA carries a true per-step peak under the same name. The MPS test at test_mps_profiling.py:70-72 pins only that the value captures a ~1 GiB transient and exceeds current allocation, which is consistent with the reserved high-water and does not pin per-step semantics. This is a documentation/labelling defect on a profiling field with no correctness or privacy consequence; exact_peak=True is defensible on its own documented meaning (a precise, transient-capturing measurement) but reinforces the wrong impression.
verdicts.corrected_failure_scenario: On MPS, StepPerf.memory_peak_gb is torch.mps.driver_allocated_memory() - the driver's monotone reserved high-water since process start - because step_perf never resets the peak counter there (peak_memory_trackable is CUDA-only). Its public docstring calls it 'Peak GPU memory during the step', so a user logging sp.perf.to_dict(prefix='train/') each step reads a run-cumulative figure as if it were a per-step peak: step-to-step comparisons are meaningless, a change that genuinely halves a step's usage shows no movement, and the same field name means something different on CUDA. Cosmetic/diagnostic only - no effect on training, clipping, noise, or accounting. Fix is to correct the StepPerf docstring (and ideally expose the CUDA/MPS distinction on the record) rather than change the measurement.
